content:
One verse in Surah Yunus gets quoted more than almost any other in the debate over the Bible. It tells the Prophet that if he is in doubt, he should ask the people who were reading the scripture before him. Read on its own, it can sound like the Quran handing the final word to the Bible.

Read with the 5 verses around it and the commentators who explained it first, it says something narrower. These 6 points go through the verse, who it speaks to, what was to be asked and of whom, and the Christian case built on it. Each point is graded. The wider argument is in The Islamic Dilemma; this article stays with one verse.

Here is the verse in Arabic:

فَإِن كُنتَ فِي شَكّٖ مِّمَّآ أَنزَلۡنَآ إِلَيۡكَ فَسۡـَٔلِ ٱلَّذِينَ يَقۡرَءُونَ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ مِن قَبۡلِكَۚ لَقَدۡ جَآءَكَ ٱلۡحَقُّ مِن رَّبِّكَ فَلَا تَكُونَنَّ مِنَ ٱلۡمُمۡتَرِينَ

In English: "So if you are in doubt, [O Muḥammad], about that which We have revealed to you, then ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you. The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord, so never be among the doubters" (Quran 10:94).[1]

The verse before it says God settled the Children of Israel "in an agreeable settlement" and that "they did not differ until [after] knowledge had come to them" (10:93). The verse after it says, "never be of those who deny the signs of Allāh and [thus] be among the losers" (10:95).[1]

So the command to ask is wrapped on both sides. Before it comes a claim about the Israelites. After it comes a second warning against doubt. A reader who quotes only the middle has cut away the two sentences that tell him what the middle is for.

Strength: strong. Both sides quote the same wording, and the context is printed beside it.

The verse opens with in, "if". The commentators read the condition as one that was never met. Al-Ṭabarī (d. 310/923) asks the obvious question himself: was the Prophet in doubt about what God told him? His answer is no, "and so said a group of the people of knowledge".[2]

He then gives the reports. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said, "the Prophet did not doubt and did not ask". Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said the same. Qatāda said, "it reached us" that the Prophet said, "I do not doubt and I do not ask". Ibn Kathīr (d. 774/1373) quotes Qatāda and adds that Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḥasan said likewise.[2][3]

I should be precise about the chains. In al-Ṭabarī the sentence "he did not doubt and did not ask" comes from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḥasan, and Qatāda gives no chain to the Prophet, so his report is mursal. What al-Ṭabarī attributes to Ibn ʿAbbās is a different line, which comes in point 4. Ibn Kathīr is the one who puts Ibn ʿAbbās with the others.[2][3]

Al-Ṭabarī explains the grammar with ordinary Arabic speech. A master says to his slave, "if you are my slave, obey me", and neither of them doubts it. He points to 5:116, where God asks Jesus whether he told people to take him and his mother as gods, though God knew he had not. He then allows a second reading: the Prophet is addressed, and the people meant are those among the believers whose conviction was still weak.[2] Ibn Kathīr says the verse is a steadying of the umma.[3]

Strength: strong. The reading is early and widely held. The Prophet-level report rests on a mursal line, and that is the honest limit.

The thing the verse asks about is "that which We have revealed to you". The nearest revealed text is the story just told: Israel crossed the sea, Pharaoh followed, believed as he drowned, and was told that his body would be kept as a sign (10:90–92).[1]

Al-Ṭabarī ties the doubt more tightly to the verse just before it. He paraphrases: if you are in doubt about what We revealed to you, that the Children of Israel did not differ over your prophethood before you were sent, because they find you written in their Torah and Gospel, then ask.[2] On his reading the question is about the Prophet himself, and the answer lies with people who knew their books.

Either way, the subject is narrow. It is a story, or a description, that the earlier readers would recognise. The Bible does tell of the crossing, and of Pharaoh's army: "There remained not so much as one of them" (Exodus 14:28).[4] Exodus does not record a deathbed confession by Pharaoh. The verse sends the Prophet to readers who would know the core of the story, and the Quran still tells it in its own way.

Strength: moderate. The context supports a narrow question. The commentators differ on which part of the context is meant, and the verse itself does not name it.

Who were "those who have been reading the Scripture before you"? Al-Ṭabarī says: people of the Torah and the Gospel "such as ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his like, of the people of truthfulness and faith in you among them", as against those among them who lied and rejected him.[5]

He gives the early reports behind that. Ibn Jurayj says Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as the people of the Torah and the Gospel "who reached Muhammad and believed in him". Ibn Zayd says, "it is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām; he was of the People of the Book, and he believed in the Messenger of God". Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says it means the God-fearing believers among them who lived to meet the Prophet. Mujāhid says only, "they are the People of the Book".[5]

The Quran uses the same appeal elsewhere. It asks whether it is not a sign "that it is recognized by the scholars of the Children of Israel" (26:197), and it speaks of "a witness from the Children of Israel" who testified and believed (46:10).[6] The witnesses are named people with a testimony. The verse makes no blanket appeal to a library.

Strength: moderate. Most early reports point to converts, Mujāhid's broader line is also on record, and one could object that Abdullah ibn Salam accepted Islam in Medina while Surah Yunus is usually counted as Meccan. Al-Ṭabarī does not raise that problem.

The verse tells the Prophet to ask people. It says nothing about which books are in a canon, which manuscripts are sound, or how a disagreement between the two scriptures is to be settled.

That last question the Quran answers somewhere else. It calls itself "confirming that which preceded it of the Scripture and as a criterion over it", and the word for criterion, muhaymin, sets the Quran above what came before (5:48).[6] The direction runs one way. A verse about asking a witness cannot reverse a verse about which book judges the other.

The same form of command appears in 16:43, "ask the people of the message if you do not know", where the subject is whether earlier messengers were men.[6] There the question asked is a single fact, and it is answered in the same verse. The word for scripture, al-kitāb, also carries more than one sense in the Quran (see What does kitab mean in the Quran?).

Al-Fārūqī's line is useful here. Islam honours what God revealed to the earlier prophets and examines the texts that later communities accepted as scripture.[7] A witness who knew those texts can confirm a description in them. That is a long way from saying the texts, as a whole, judge the Quran. The question of what the Quran says about their state is treated in Did Islam teach that the Bible was corrupted?.

Strength: strong. The verse speaks of asking; 5:48 speaks of judging; the Quran keeps them apart.

Here is the case at its best. The verse is God speaking to the Prophet. If the Prophet ever doubted, God sent him to the readers of the earlier scripture to settle it. A source you consult to cure doubt is a source you trust. So the Quran treats the Jewish and Christian scriptures of the seventh century as a reliable check, and those scriptures are, in substance, the Bible we still read. Where the Quran and that Bible disagree, the argument runs, the verse itself tells you which to believe.

There is real force in one part of this. The verse would make little sense if the earlier readers had nothing true to report. The Quran does assume that people of the book could recognise truth from their own scripture, and a Muslim should say so plainly.

The rest does not hold. The argument needs the condition to have been met, and the earliest commentators say it was not. It needs the question to be open-ended, and the context and al-Ṭabarī make it a narrow one. It needs "those who read" to mean any reader of any copy, and the tafsir names believers like Abdullah ibn Salam. And it needs the verse to outrank 5:48, which calls the Quran the criterion over what came before. A related case, which turns the same test back on the New Testament, is in The Christian twin of the Islamic Dilemma.

Strength of the Christian argument: weak. It shows that the Quran expects the earlier scripture to carry true witness, and it stops there.

The bottom line

Quran 10:94 is a conditional spoken to a Prophet who, by the early reports, neither doubted nor asked. It points to a narrow question about the story just told or about the Prophet's description, and to named witnesses who believed. Read that way, it fits the rest of the Quran, which confirms the earlier books and is the criterion over them.

The Christian reading takes one true thing, that the earlier scripture still carried witness, and asks it to carry far more than the verse says. Allāhu aʿlam.
